question: A pipe can fill a tank in 27 hours. Another pipe can empty the filled tank in 28 hours. If both the pipes are opened simultaneously, then the time (in hours) in which the tank will be one-fourth filled, is:
solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let filling pipe be **A** and emptying pipe be **B**.

Net efficiency for filling full tank = (1/27 − 1/28) = 1/(27 × 28) per hour.

Time to fill full tank = 27 × 28 = 756 hours.

Time to fill 1/4th tank = 756 ÷ 4 = 189 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 189 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

 **Pipe**
 **Time (hrs)**
 **Total Work (LCM)**
 **Efficiency**

 **Pipe A (Inlet)**
 27
 756
 +28

 **Pipe B (Outlet)**
 28

⇒ **Total Capacity** of tank = LCM of 27 and 28 = 756 units.

⇒ Efficiency of **Pipe A** = 756 ÷ 27 = +28 units/hr.

⇒ Efficiency of **Pipe B** = 756 ÷ 28 = −27 units/hr.

⇒ Combined efficiency (A + B) = 28 − 27 = 1 unit/hr.

⇒ Work to be done = 1/4 of total capacity = 756 ÷ 4 = 189 units.

⇒ Required Time = 189 ÷ 1 = 189 hours.

**∴ The correct answer is 189 hours.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

Inlet and Outlet Pipes

Inlet pipe efficiency is taken as **positive (+)** and outlet (emptying) pipe efficiency is taken as **negative (−)**.

Net Time Formula

If an inlet fills in 'x' hours and outlet empties in 'y' hours, net time to fill is **(xy) ÷ (y − x)**, provided y > x.</p
